proof:
**Step 1.** Let T and U be the areas of two triangles whose bases have lengths b and c and whose heights are equal. Superpose their equal perpendicular heights on the same segment AO; this changes neither their areas nor their base lengths (D6.4; CN4). Their base-lines coincide in a straight line ℓ, since both are perpendicular to AO at O (1.14). Through A draw the parallel p to ℓ (1.31). Both triangles are therefore between ℓ and p.

**Step 2.** Let m and n be arbitrary positive integers. Starting from O along one ray of ℓ, lay off successive segments OX₁, X₁X₂, …, Xₘ₋₁Xₘ, each equal to b. Independently, along the same ray, lay off OY₁, Y₁Y₂, …, Yₙ₋₁Yₙ, each equal to c. These constructions are made by producing the line and repeatedly cutting off a segment equal to the given base (P2; 1.3). Join A to all the division points (P1). By the definition of a multiple, OXₘ = mb and OYₙ = nc (D5.2).

**Step 3.** Every triangle on one of the successive b-segments with vertex A equals T: its base equals b, and it lies between the same parallels ℓ and p as the original triangle. Likewise, every triangle on one of the successive c-segments with vertex A equals U (1.38). The first collection partitions triangle AOXₘ, and the second partitions triangle AOYₙ. Adding these equal areas therefore gives area(AOXₘ) = mT and area(AOYₙ) = nU (CN2; D5.2).

**Step 4.** Compare OXₘ and OYₙ. If OXₘ is greater, Yₙ lies between O and Xₘ, so triangle AOYₙ is a proper part of triangle AOXₘ; hence mT > nU (CN5). If the segments are equal, Xₘ and Yₙ coincide, so the triangles coincide and mT = nU (CN4). If OXₘ is less, the same proper-part argument with the triangles interchanged gives mT < nU (CN5). Thus mT and nU have exactly the same comparison as mb and nc.

**Step 5.** Since m and n were arbitrary, the equimultiple definition of equal ratios gives T:U = b:c (D5.5). This direct route makes no assumption that the bases have a common measure. The assertion for triangles is proved.

**Step 6.** Now let P and Q be the areas of two parallelograms with respective bases b and c and equal heights. Use diagonal bisection, since it supplies the required half-triangles directly: draw a diagonal in each parallelogram (P1), and let T′ and U′ be the areas of the resulting triangles having the specified bases. Each diagonal bisects its parallelogram, so P = 2T′ and Q = 2U′ (1.34). These triangles have the respective bases b and c and retain the common height of the parallelograms (D6.4).

**Step 7.** Equimultiples have the same ratio as the original magnitudes, so P:Q = (2T′):(2U′) = T′:U′ (5.15). By Step 5, T′:U′ = b:c. Consequently P:Q = b:c (5.11). Therefore triangles of the same height are to one another as their bases, and parallelograms of the same height are likewise to one another as their bases.
statement: Triangles and parallelograms which are under the same height are to one another as their bases.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let ABC be a triangle, with D in the interior of AB and E in the interior of AC. Join DE, BE, and CD. Write [XYZ] for the area of triangle XYZ. We shall prove that DE is parallel to BC if and only if BD:DA = CE:EA. [P1]

**Step 2.** Triangles BDE and ADE, with bases BD and DA on AB, have the same perpendicular height from E. Likewise, triangles CDE and ADE, with bases CE and EA on AC, have the same perpendicular height from D. Hence
[BDE]:[ADE] = BD:DA,
and
[CDE]:[ADE] = CE:EA.
[D6.4, 6.1]

**Step 3.** First suppose DE is parallel to BC. Triangles BDE and CDE are on the same base DE and between the same parallels DE and BC. Therefore [BDE] = [CDE]. The common base makes the same-base area theorem the direct choice. [1.37]

**Step 4.** Equal magnitudes have the same ratio to the same magnitude, so
[BDE]:[ADE] = [CDE]:[ADE]. [5.7]
Combining this equality with the two proportions in Step 2 gives BD:DA = CE:EA. [5.11]
Thus the sides AB and AC are cut proportionally. [D5.6]

**Step 5.** Conversely, suppose BD:DA = CE:EA. The proportions established in Step 2 then give
[BDE]:[ADE] = [CDE]:[ADE]. [5.11]

**Step 6.** Magnitudes having the same ratio to the same magnitude are equal. Consequently [BDE] = [CDE]. [5.9]

**Step 7.** Since D and E lie inside AB and AC respectively, B and C are on the same side of DE. Thus BDE and CDE are equal triangles on the same base DE and on the same side of it. The straight line BC joining their remaining vertices is therefore parallel to DE. The same-base converse applies directly here. [1.39]
Together with Step 4, this proves both assertions.
statement: If a straight line be drawn parallel to one of the sides of a triangle, it will cut the sides of the triangle proportionally; and, if the sides of the triangle be cut proportionally, the line joining the points of section will be parallel to the remaining side of the triangle.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let ABC be a triangle, and let D lie between B and C. Join AD (P1). We must prove that ∠BAD = ∠DAC if and only if BD:DC = AB:AC. Path choice: use one auxiliary parallel and 6.2, which directly supplies the required ratio of segments and serves both implications.

**Step 2.** Produce BA beyond A to X (P2). Through C draw a straight line parallel to AD (1.31), and let CY be its ray on the side of AC opposite B. By 1.29, ∠ACY = ∠DAC. By 1.13, ∠XAC + ∠BAC equals two right angles. Since ∠DAC is a proper part of ∠BAC, it is smaller (CN5); consequently ∠XAC + ∠ACY is less than two right angles. Therefore AX and CY, produced if necessary, meet at E on that side of AC (P5). Thus B, A, E are collinear, A lies between B and E, and CE is parallel to AD.

**Step 3.** In triangle BEC, the straight line AD is parallel to the side EC and cuts BE and BC at A and D. Hence
BA:AE = BD:DC.
This is precisely the proportional division supplied by 6.2.

**Step 4.** Since AD is parallel to CE and B, A, E lie in that order on one straight line, the corresponding angles give ∠BAD = ∠AEC. With AC as transversal, the alternate angles give ∠DAC = ∠ACE (1.29).

**Step 5.** First suppose that AD bisects ∠BAC, so that ∠BAD = ∠DAC. The equalities in Step 4 yield ∠AEC = ∠ACE (CN1). Therefore the sides opposite these equal angles in triangle AEC are equal: AE = AC (1.6). Here 1.6 applies directly because equality of angles has already been established.

**Step 6.** Since AE = AC, the same magnitude AB has the same ratio to them: AB:AE = AB:AC (5.7). Combining this with Step 3 gives
BD:DC = AB:AC
(5.11). This proves the first implication.

**Step 7.** Conversely, suppose that BD:DC = AB:AC. Step 3 also gives BD:DC = AB:AE; hence AB:AE = AB:AC (5.11). Magnitudes to which the same magnitude has the same ratio are equal, so AE = AC (5.9).

**Step 8.** In triangle AEC, the equality AE = AC gives ∠AEC = ∠ACE (1.5). Combining this with the angle equalities in Step 4 yields ∠BAD = ∠DAC (CN1). Thus AD bisects ∠BAC. Both implications are proved.
statement: If an angle of a triangle be bisected and the straight line cutting the angle cut the base also, the segments of the base will have the same ratio as the remaining sides of the triangle; and, if the segments of the base have the same ratio as the remaining sides of the triangle, the straight line joined from the vertex to the point of section will bisect the angle of the triangle.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let ABC and DEF be equiangular triangles, with ∠BAC = ∠EDF, ∠ABC = ∠DEF, and ∠ACB = ∠DFE. We first prove AB : AC = DE : DF. The chosen route is a parallel cut, since 6.2 directly supplies the needed segment proportions.

**Step 2.** Interchanging the triangles if necessary, suppose AB ≥ DE; this merely interchanges the two sides of the desired equality of ratios. If AB = DE, the equal angles at A, B and D, E give AC = DF and BC = EF by 1.26. All the required proportions then follow from equality of corresponding magnitudes and D5.5. It remains to consider AB > DE.

**Step 3.** Cut off AP = DE on AB, with P between A and B [1.3]. Through P draw PQ parallel to BC, meeting AC at Q, between A and C [1.31].

**Step 4.** Since AP and AQ lie along AB and AC, ∠PAQ = ∠BAC [CN4]. Also ∠APQ = ∠ABC because PQ is parallel to BC [1.29]. Hence ∠PAQ = ∠EDF and ∠APQ = ∠DEF by the given angle equalities [CN1]. Together with AP = DE, these equalities give AQ = DF by 1.26.

**Step 5.** Because PQ is parallel to BC, it cuts the other two sides proportionally:
AP : PB = AQ : QC [6.2].
Alternating gives
AP : AQ = PB : QC [5.16].

**Step 6.** By 5.12, the ratio of the sums of these antecedents and consequents equals their common ratio:
(AP + PB) : (AQ + QC) = AP : AQ.
Since AP + PB = AB and AQ + QC = AC, this is AB : AC = AP : AQ. Substituting AP = DE and AQ = DF gives
AB : AC = DE : DF [D5.5].
Here 5.12 is the direct choice because the sums are precisely the two whole sides required.

**Step 7.** The argument in Steps 2–6 applies to any chosen pair of corresponding vertices. Applying it with (A, B, C; D, E, F) relabelled as (B, A, C; E, D, F), and then as (C, A, B; F, D, E), gives respectively
BA : BC = ED : EF,
and
CA : CB = FD : FE.
Thus the sides about every pair of equal angles are proportional [D5.6].

**Step 8.** The corresponding terms in these proportions pair AB with DE, AC with DF, and BC with EF [D5.11]. These pairs subtend, respectively, the equal angles at C and F, at B and E, and at A and D. Therefore, in equiangular triangles the sides about the equal angles are proportional, and the corresponding sides are those which subtend the equal angles.
statement: In equiangular triangles the sides about the equal angles are proportional, and those are corresponding sides which subtend the equal angles.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let ABC and DEF be triangles whose corresponding sides are AB and DE, BC and EF, and CA and FD. By hypothesis their sides are proportional; thus AB:BC = DE:EF and BC:CA = EF:FD. We must prove that their corresponding angles are equal. [Hypothesis; D5.6]

**Step 2.** We choose an equiangular auxiliary triangle on EF, so that 6.4 will supply proportions involving this shared side. At E and F, on the same side of EF, construct angles GEF and EFG equal respectively to ABC and BCA. [1.23] Since angles ABC and BCA together are less than two right angles, the constructed arms meet on that side of EF at a point G. [1.17; P5]

**Step 3.** The sums of the angles of triangles ABC and GEF are equal, since each equals two right angles. [1.32; CN1] The two pairs of copied angles have equal sums. [CN2] Subtracting these equal sums gives ∠BAC = ∠EGF. Consequently ABC and GEF are equiangular, with A corresponding to G, B to E, and C to F. [CN3]

**Step 4.** The sides opposite the equal angles in these equiangular triangles are proportional. Hence AB:BC = GE:EF and BC:CA = EF:FG. [6.4]

**Step 5.** Comparing these proportions with the hypothesis, ratios equal to the same ratio are equal to one another. Therefore DE:EF = GE:EF and EF:FD = EF:FG. [5.11]

**Step 6.** Apply 5.9 directly: the first equality of ratios has the same consequent EF, so DE = GE; the second has the same antecedent EF, so FD = FG. Thus triangles DEF and GEF have all three corresponding sides equal, EF being common. [5.9]

**Step 7.** Applying the side–side–side angle-equality proposition at each corresponding vertex gives ∠EDF = ∠EGF, ∠DEF = ∠GEF, and ∠DFE = ∠GFE. This is the direct next step because all three corresponding sides have just been shown equal. [1.8]

**Step 8.** Combining these equalities with the copied angles and the remaining-angle equality from Step 3 yields ∠BAC = ∠EDF, ∠ABC = ∠DEF, and ∠ACB = ∠DFE. These are respectively the angles subtended by the corresponding sides BC and EF, CA and FD, and AB and DE. Therefore the given triangles are equiangular, and the angles subtended by corresponding sides are equal. [CN1]
statement: If two triangles have their sides proportional, the triangles will be equiangular and will have those angles equal which the corresponding sides subtend.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let ABC and DEF be triangles such that ∠BAC = ∠EDF and AB:AC = DE:DF, with AB corresponding to DE and AC to DF. These are the given hypotheses.

**Step 2.** At E construct a ray on the same side of DE as F, making with ED an angle equal to ∠ABC [1.23]. The sum ∠BAC + ∠ABC is less than two right angles [1.17]. Since ∠EDF = ∠BAC, the constructed ray and the ray DF therefore meet on that side of DE [P5], producing the straight lines as necessary [P2]. Call their intersection G. Thus ∠DEG = ∠ABC, and G lies on the ray DF.

**Step 3.** Since DG and DF have the same direction, ∠EDG = ∠EDF [CN4], and hence ∠EDG = ∠BAC [CN1]. Together with ∠DEG = ∠ABC, this gives ∠DGE = ∠ACB: the angles of each triangle sum to two right angles, and subtracting the equal sums of the first two angles leaves equal third angles [1.32, CN2, CN3]. Thus triangles ABC and DEG are equiangular.

**Step 4.** Path choice: apply 6.4 directly to these equiangular triangles, obtaining AB:AC = DE:DG [6.4]. But AB:AC = DE:DF by hypothesis. Therefore DE:DG = DE:DF, since ratios equal to the same ratio are equal to one another [5.11].

**Step 5.** Since DE has the same ratio to DG and DF, the latter magnitudes are equal: DG = DF [5.9]. Both G and F lie on the same ray from D. If they were distinct, one of DG and DF would be a proper part of the other and therefore smaller, contrary to their equality [CN5]. Hence G and F coincide.

**Step 6.** Consequently, the angle equalities established for DEG give ∠ABC = ∠DEF and ∠ACB = ∠DFE [CN4, CN1]. Together with the given equality ∠BAC = ∠EDF, these show that ABC and DEF are equiangular. The equal angles at C and F are opposite the corresponding sides AB and DE; those at B and E are opposite AC and DF; and those at A and D are opposite BC and EF. Thus the angles subtended by corresponding sides are equal, as required.
statement: If two triangles have one angle equal to one angle and the sides about the equal angles proportional, the triangles will be equiangular and will have those angles equal which the corresponding sides subtend.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let ABC and DEF be the given triangles, with ∠BAC = ∠EDF and AB:BC = DE:EF. Suppose that the remaining angles ∠ACB and ∠DFE are either both less than a right angle or both not less than a right angle. These are the hypotheses. Write R for a right angle; all right angles are equal. [P4]

**Step 2.** If ∠ABC = ∠DEF, the remaining angles are also equal, by subtracting the two pairs of equal angles from the angle sums of the triangles, and the conclusion follows. [1.32, CN3] Suppose, therefore, that ∠ABC and ∠DEF are unequal. Interchanging the triangles if necessary, assume ∠ABC > ∠DEF.

**Step 3.** At B construct a ray BG inside ∠ABC such that ∠ABG = ∠DEF. [1.23] Since ∠ABG < ∠ABC, we have ∠BAC + ∠ABG < ∠BAC + ∠ABC < 2R. [CN5, 1.17] Consequently this ray meets AC on the side of AB containing C. [P5] Because the ray lies strictly inside ∠ABC, its intersection G lies strictly between A and C.

**Step 4.** Since AG lies along AC, ∠BAG = ∠BAC = ∠EDF. [CN4, hypothesis] Together with ∠ABG = ∠DEF, this gives ∠AGB = ∠DFE by the angle sums of triangles ABG and DEF. [1.32, CN3] Thus those triangles are equiangular.

**Step 5.** Path choice: apply 6.4, since the auxiliary triangles have already been shown equiangular. It gives AB:BG = DE:EF. [6.4] Combining this with the given proportion AB:BC = DE:EF yields AB:BG = AB:BC. [5.11] Therefore BG = BC, since magnitudes to which the same magnitude has the same ratio are equal. [5.9]

**Step 6.** Triangle BGC is consequently isosceles, so ∠BGC = ∠GCB. [1.5] Since G lies between A and C, ∠GCB = ∠ACB. [CN4] The two equal base angles of BGC have sum less than 2R. [1.17] Hence each is less than R: otherwise both would be at least R and their sum would be at least 2R. [P4, CN2, CN5] In particular, ∠ACB < R.

**Step 7.** Since A, G, C lie on one straight line, ∠AGB + ∠BGC = 2R. [1.13] As ∠BGC < R, its supplementary angle ∠AGB is greater than R. [P4, CN3, CN5] But ∠AGB = ∠DFE by Step 4, whereas ∠ACB < R by Step 6. Thus one of the original remaining angles is less than a right angle and the other is greater than a right angle, contradicting either permitted alternative in the hypothesis.

**Step 8.** Therefore ∠ABC = ∠DEF. Together with the given equality ∠BAC = ∠EDF, the angle sums now give ∠ACB = ∠DFE. [1.32, CN3] Hence ABC and DEF are equiangular, and in particular the angles ABC and DEF, about which the given proportional sides lie, are equal. This proves the proposition.
statement: If two triangles have one angle equal to one angle, the sides about other angles proportional, and the remaining angles either both less or both not less than a right angle, the triangles will be equiangular and will have those angles equal, the sides about which are proportional.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let ABC be a triangle right-angled at A, and let the given perpendicular AD meet the base BC at D. The angles BDA and ADC are right angles, so each equals the right angle BAC. [D1.10, P4]

**Step 2.** Since D lies on BC, the angles DBA and ABC coincide and are therefore equal. [CN4] The angle sums of triangles DBA and ABC are equal, each being two right angles. Subtracting their equal right angles and then their equal angles at B gives ∠BAD = ∠BCA. Thus triangles DBA and ABC are equiangular, with correspondence D ↔ A, B ↔ B, A ↔ C. [1.32, CN1, CN3]

**Step 3.** Path choice: apply 6.4 directly, since angle equalities have already been established. The sides about the equal angles of triangles DBA and ABC are proportional; hence these triangles are similar. [6.4, D6.1]

**Step 4.** Likewise, the angles DCA and BCA coincide and are equal. [CN4] The angle sums of triangles DAC and ABC are equal, each being two right angles. Subtracting their equal right angles and then their equal angles at C gives ∠DAC = ∠ABC. [1.32, CN1, CN3] Consequently, triangles DAC and ABC are equiangular, with correspondence D ↔ A, A ↔ B, C ↔ C. Their sides about the equal angles are therefore proportional, and they are similar. [6.4, D6.1]

**Step 5.** The two smaller triangles are also equiangular: ∠BDA = ∠ADC because both are right angles; ∠DBA = ∠DAC because both equal ∠ABC; and ∠BAD = ∠DCA because both equal ∠BCA. Their correspondence is therefore D ↔ D, B ↔ A, A ↔ C. [P4, CN1; Steps 2 and 4]

**Step 6.** Applying 6.4 to triangles DBA and DAC, their sides about the equal angles are proportional; hence they are similar. [6.4, D6.1] Thus the triangles adjoining the perpendicular are similar both to the whole triangle and to one another, as required.
statement: If in a right-angled triangle a perpendicular be drawn from the right angle to the base, the triangles adjoining the perpendicular are similar both to the whole and to one another.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let AB be the given straight line, and let the prescribed part be its nth part, where n ≥ 2. We must construct a segment which, repeated n times, equals AB; this is the required part in the sense of D5.1 and D5.2.

**Step 2.** Draw from A a straight line not lying along AB, and produce it as necessary. On it mark successive points A₁, A₂, …, Aₙ so that AA₁, A₁A₂, …, Aₙ₋₁Aₙ are all equal: each successive point is obtained by a circle centered at the preceding point with the fixed radius AA₁, taking the intersection in the forward direction [P1, P2, P3, D1.15]. Put E = A₁ and C = Aₙ. Then E lies between A and C, and AC is the sum of n copies of AE, so AC = n·AE [CN2, D5.2].

**Step 3.** Join CB. Through E draw a straight line parallel to CB, meeting AB at D, between A and B [P1, 1.31].

**Step 4.** In triangle ACB, the parallel ED cuts the sides proportionally. Hence CE:EA = BD:DA [6.2]. This is the direct path: the constructed parallel immediately supplies the required proportion, without an additional angle or similarity argument.

**Step 5.** By composition of the proportion in Step 4, (CE + EA):EA = (BD + DA):DA. Since these sums are CA and BA respectively, AC:AE = AB:AD [5.18].

**Step 6.** Apply the definition of equal ratios to this proportion, taking one copy of each antecedent and n copies of each consequent. Since AC equals n·AE by Step 2, AB must likewise equal n·AD [D5.5]. Thus AD measures AB exactly n times, and, since D lies between A and B, AD is the prescribed nth part cut off from AB [D5.1, D5.2].
statement: From a given straight line to cut off a prescribed part.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let AB be the given uncut straight line, and let CD be divided at the points C₁, …, Cₙ₋₁, in that order; write C₀ = C and Cₙ = D. From A draw a straight line AX, not collinear with AB, and produce it until it is longer than CD (P1, P2). On AX take points P₁, …, Pₙ such that APᵢ = CCᵢ for each i, and put P₀ = A (1.3). These points occur in the same order as the given division points. Subtracting equal initial segments gives Pᵢ₋₁Pᵢ = Cᵢ₋₁Cᵢ for every i; for i = 1 this is already a construction equality (CN3).

**Step 2.** Join PₙB (P1). Through each Pᵢ, for 1 ≤ i < n, draw a straight line parallel to PₙB, meeting the side AB at Qᵢ (1.31). Put Q₀ = A and Qₙ = B. These are the proposed division points of AB.

**Step 3.** Path choice: use the proportional cutting theorem directly, since the construction supplies parallels to a side of a triangle; introducing equiangular triangles is unnecessary. In triangle APₙB, the parallel PᵢQᵢ gives
APᵢ : PᵢPₙ = AQᵢ : QᵢB
for every 1 ≤ i < n (6.2).

**Step 4.** Taking these proportions jointly gives
APₙ : PᵢPₙ = AB : QᵢB
(5.18). Alternating therefore gives
PᵢPₙ : QᵢB = APₙ : AB
(5.16). The same equality holds for i = 0, since P₀ = Q₀ = A. Thus every nonzero terminal segment on APₙ has to its corresponding terminal segment on AB the same ratio APₙ : AB.

**Step 5.** Fix any i with 1 ≤ i < n. By Step 4, the two successive terminal-segment ratios are equal:
Pᵢ₋₁Pₙ : Qᵢ₋₁B = PᵢPₙ : QᵢB
(5.11). Remove the latter pair of segments from the former pair. The remainders have the same ratio as the wholes (5.19), so
Pᵢ₋₁Pᵢ : Qᵢ₋₁Qᵢ = APₙ : AB.
For i = n, this equality is already the terminal-segment equality in Step 4 with index n − 1. Consequently it holds for every corresponding pair of individual segments.

**Step 6.** For any two indices i and j, Step 5 gives
Pᵢ₋₁Pᵢ : Qᵢ₋₁Qᵢ = Pⱼ₋₁Pⱼ : Qⱼ₋₁Qⱼ
(5.11). Alternating yields
Pᵢ₋₁Pᵢ : Pⱼ₋₁Pⱼ = Qᵢ₋₁Qᵢ : Qⱼ₋₁Qⱼ
(5.16). Replacing the auxiliary segments by the equal given segments established in Step 1 gives
Cᵢ₋₁Cᵢ : Cⱼ₋₁Cⱼ = Qᵢ₋₁Qᵢ : Qⱼ₋₁Qⱼ
(5.7, 5.11). Thus the segments of AB, in their corresponding order, are proportional to the segments of CD (D5.6). Therefore AB has been cut similarly to the given cut straight line CD, as required.
statement: To cut a given uncut straight line similarly to a given cut straight line.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let the two given straight lines have lengths a and b. Draw two noncollinear rays from A. On the first mark B and C, in the order A, B, C, so that AB = a and BC = b; on the second mark D so that AD = b. These placements are made by transferring the given lengths and cutting them off on the rays, produced as necessary. [P1, P2, 1.2, 1.3]

**Step 2.** Join BD. Through C draw a straight line ℓ parallel to BD. [P1, 1.31]

**Step 3.** The ray of ℓ on the side of AC containing D makes with CA an angle equal to ∠ABD. [1.29] But ∠BAD and ∠ABD together are less than two right angles. [1.17] Therefore ℓ meets the ray AD at a point E on that side of AC. [P5] Moreover, E lies beyond D: if E were D, or were between A and D, the segment CE would meet BD, in the latter case by entering triangle ABD across BD. This is impossible because ℓ is parallel to BD. [D1.23]

**Step 4.** In triangle ACE, B lies on AC, D lies on AE, and BD is parallel to CE. Hence AB : BC = AD : DE. [6.2] This is the direct path: the parallel gives the required ratio of the side-segments immediately, without passing through equiangular triangles.

**Step 5.** Substituting AB = a, BC = b, and AD = b into that proportion gives a : b = b : DE; replacing magnitudes by equal magnitudes preserves the defining comparisons of their equimultiples. [D5.5] Thus the given first line, the given second line, and DE are continuously proportional. Therefore DE is the required third proportional. [D5.6]
statement: To two given straight lines to find a third proportional.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let the three given straight lines, in their given order, be a, b, and c. We must construct a straight line x such that a:b = c:x (D5.6). We choose the parallel-cut construction: 6.2 naturally applies first because it gives the required ratio directly between segments of two sides.

**Step 2.** Draw two rays from O which do not lie in one straight line. On the first mark A and B, in the order O, A, B, so that OA = a and AB = b. On the second mark C so that OC = c. These lengths are cut off after producing the straight lines sufficiently (P1, P2, 1.3).

**Step 3.** Join AC. Through B draw a straight line ℓ parallel to AC (P1, 1.31).

**Step 4.** The ray of ℓ on the same side of OB as C makes with BO an angle equal to ∠OAC (1.29). In triangle OAC, the angles ∠AOC and ∠OAC together are less than two right angles (1.17). Therefore ℓ meets the ray OC at a point D on that side of OB (P5). Moreover, D lies beyond C: if it were at C, or between O and C, BD would meet AC, contrary to their being parallel (D1.23).

**Step 5.** In triangle OBD, A lies on OB and C lies on OD, and AC is parallel to BD. Hence the sides are cut proportionally:
OA:AB = OC:CD (6.2).

**Step 6.** Substituting the equalities constructed in Step 2 into the proportion of Step 5 gives a:b = c:CD. Thus CD is a fourth proportional to the three given straight lines, as required (D5.6).
statement: To three given straight lines to find a fourth proportional.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let AB be the first given straight line. Produce AB beyond B sufficiently far, and cut off BC equal to the second given straight line, so that A, B, C lie in this order on one straight line. [P2, 1.3]

**Step 2.** Bisect AC at O, and describe the circle with centre O and radius OA. Since OA = OC, both A and C lie on the circle, and AC is a diameter. [1.10, P3, D1.15, D1.17]

**Step 3.** At B construct a perpendicular to AC, and produce it to meet the circle at D on either side of AC. Join AD and CD. The angles ABD and DBC are right angles. [1.11, P2, P1, D1.10]

**Step 4.** Since AC is a diameter, the angle ADC is an angle in a semicircle and is therefore right. Thus DB is the perpendicular from the right-angle vertex of triangle ADC to its opposite side AC. [3.31; Step 3] The direct path is now the right-triangle altitude similarity of 6.8, whose configuration has been constructed exactly.

**Step 5.** By 6.8, triangles ABD and DBC are similar both to triangle ADC and to one another. Their correspondence is (A, B, D) ↔ (D, B, C): their right-angle vertices are B, while their angles at A and C respectively coincide with the corresponding angles of the whole triangle. Hence their corresponding sides about the right angles are proportional:
AB : BD = BD : BC. [6.8, D6.1]

**Step 6.** AB is the first given straight line, and BC equals the second. Replacing BC by that equal given line leaves the ratio unchanged. Therefore the first given straight line is to BD as BD is to the second given straight line. Thus BD is the required mean proportional. [Step 1, D5.5, D5.6]
statement: To two given straight lines to find a mean proportional.

proof:
**Step 1.** Choose corresponding equal angles of the two parallelograms. Place their vertices together at O and their corresponding arms along the same two rays. Denote the parallelograms, in cyclic order, by OABC and ODEF, with A and D on one ray and C and F on the other. This placement preserves lengths and areas by coincidence (CN4). The required reciprocal proportion is OA:OD = OF:OC (D6.2).

**Step 2.** Let the straight lines BC and DE, produced if necessary, meet at G (P2). This intersection exists: BC is parallel to OA, and DE is parallel to OC; if BC and DE were parallel, transitivity of parallelism would make OA and OC parallel (1.30), contrary to their meeting at O (D1.23). Now OD is parallel to CG, and OC is parallel to DG, so ODGC is an auxiliary parallelogram.

**Step 3.** Write p, q, and r for the areas of OABC, ODEF, and ODGC respectively. **Path choice:** compare both given parallelograms with this single auxiliary parallelogram, using the same-height theorem 6.1. The parallelograms OABC and ODGC have bases OA and OD and lie between the same parallels OA and BC. Therefore
p:r = OA:OD. (6.1)

**Step 4.** Taking OF and OC as bases, the parallelograms ODEF and ODGC lie between the same parallels OC and DE. Therefore
q:r = OF:OC. (6.1)

**Step 5.** First suppose that the given parallelograms are equal, so p = q. Equal magnitudes have the same ratio to the same magnitude; hence p:r = q:r (5.7). Combining this equality with Steps 3 and 4 gives
OA:OD = OF:OC (5.11).
Thus the sides about the chosen equal angles are reciprocally proportional (D6.2).

**Step 6.** Conversely, suppose that the sides about the corresponding equal angles are reciprocally proportional, so OA:OD = OF:OC (D6.2). Steps 3 and 4 then give p:r = q:r (5.11). Magnitudes having the same ratio to the same magnitude are equal, so p = q (5.9). Here 5.9 is the direct choice because the two area ratios have the common consequent r. Consequently the given parallelograms are equal. Both assertions are proved.
statement: In equal and equiangular parallelograms the sides about the equal angles are reciprocally proportional; and equiangular parallelograms in which the sides about the equal angles are reciprocally proportional are equal.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let ABC and DEF be triangles with ∠BAC = ∠EDF. Write [XYZ] for the area of triangle XYZ. We shall prove that [ABC] = [DEF] if and only if AB : DE = DF : AC, which expresses reciprocal proportionality of the sides about the equal angles. [D6.2]

**Step 2.** On the rays AB and AC take points G and H respectively such that AG = DE and AH = DF, extending the sides and cutting off the required lengths when necessary. If a required length equals the existing side, use its endpoint. Join GC and GH. [P2, 1.3, P1]

**Step 3.** Since AG and AH lie along AB and AC, we have ∠GAH = ∠BAC = ∠EDF. Together with AG = DE and AH = DF, this gives [AGH] = [DEF] by the side-angle-side proposition. [1.4]

**Step 4.** Path choice: use the intermediate triangle AGC to compare common-height triangles directly; the common-height theorem 6.1 applies immediately, without introducing parallelograms. Triangles ABC and AGC have bases AB and AG on the same straight line and the same vertex C. Triangles AGH and AGC have bases AH and AC on the same straight line and the same vertex G. Thus each pair has the same height, and
[ABC] : [AGC] = AB : AG,
[AGH] : [AGC] = AH : AC. [D6.4, 6.1]

**Step 5.** First suppose [ABC] = [DEF]. By Step 3, [ABC] = [AGH]. Equal magnitudes have the same ratio to the same magnitude, so
[ABC] : [AGC] = [AGH] : [AGC].
Combining this with Step 4 gives AB : AG = AH : AC. Substituting AG = DE and AH = DF yields AB : DE = DF : AC. Hence the sides about the equal angles are reciprocally proportional. [CN1, 5.7, 5.11, D6.2]

**Step 6.** Conversely, suppose AB : DE = DF : AC. Since AG = DE and AH = DF, this gives AB : AG = AH : AC. Therefore Step 4 yields
[ABC] : [AGC] = [AGH] : [AGC].
Magnitudes having the same ratio to the same magnitude are equal, so [ABC] = [AGH]. By Step 3, [AGH] = [DEF]; hence [ABC] = [DEF]. Thus the triangles are equal, and both assertions are proved. [5.7, 5.11, 5.9, CN1]
statement: In equal triangles which have one angle equal to one angle the sides about the equal angles are reciprocally proportional; and those triangles which have one angle equal to one angle, and in which the sides about the equal angles are reciprocally proportional, are equal.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let the four given straight lines, in their stated order, be a, b, c, d. Let R denote the rectangular parallelogram contained by a and d, and S the rectangular parallelogram contained by b and c. Thus R is the rectangle contained by the extremes, and S is the rectangle contained by the means (D2.1).

**Step 2.** Since all their angles are right angles, R and S are equiangular (P4). We choose 6.14 directly because it concerns equiangular parallelograms themselves, without requiring auxiliary triangles. For these rectangles, reciprocal proportionality of the sides about their equal angles is precisely a:b = c:d: a side of R is to a side of S as the remaining side of S is to the remaining side of R (D6.2).

**Step 3.** Suppose first that the four straight lines are proportional. Then a:b = c:d (D5.6). Consequently, the sides about the equal angles of R and S are reciprocally proportional, as identified in Step 2. By 6.14, R and S are equal. Hence the rectangle contained by the extremes equals the rectangle contained by the means (D2.1).

**Step 4.** Conversely, suppose that the rectangle contained by the extremes equals the rectangle contained by the means; that is, R = S (D2.1). These parallelograms are also equiangular by Step 2. Therefore, by 6.14, their sides about the equal angles are reciprocally proportional, giving a:b = c:d. Thus the four straight lines are proportional (D5.6). Both implications are proved.
statement: If four straight lines be proportional, the rectangle contained by the extremes is equal to the rectangle contained by the means; and, if the rectangle contained by the extremes be equal to the rectangle contained by the means, the four straight lines will be proportional.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let the three straight lines, in order, be a, b, c. Write R(x,y) for the rectangle contained by x and y, and S(b) for the square on b. The square on b is precisely the rectangle contained by b and b, so S(b) = R(b,b). [D1.22, D2.1] **Path choice:** apply 6.16 to the four entries a, b, b, c. Repeating the mean makes that theorem directly applicable in both directions, without an auxiliary construction.

**Step 2.** Suppose the three straight lines are proportional; that is, a:b = b:c. [D5.6] Thus the four entries a, b, b, c are proportional. By 6.16, the rectangle contained by their extremes equals the rectangle contained by their means: R(a,c) = R(b,b). By Step 1, this is R(a,c) = S(b). Therefore the rectangle contained by the extremes equals the square on the mean. [6.16, D1.22, D2.1]

**Step 3.** Conversely, suppose R(a,c) = S(b). Since S(b) is R(b,b), this says that the rectangle contained by the extremes of a, b, b, c equals the rectangle contained by their means. [D1.22, D2.1] The converse direction of 6.16 therefore gives a:b = b:c. Hence the three straight lines a, b, c are proportional. [6.16, D5.6] Both assertions are proved.
statement: If three straight lines be proportional, the rectangle contained by the extremes is equal to the square on the mean; and, if the rectangle contained by the extremes be equal to the square on the mean, the three straight lines will be proportional.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let AB be the given straight line, and let C₁C₂…Cₙ be the given rectilineal figure, with C₁C₂ chosen as the side corresponding to AB. Draw noncrossing internal diagonals dividing the figure into triangles, beginning with the triangle incident to C₁C₂ [P1]. We choose the angle-copying route: reproduce these triangles successively, so that proportionality follows directly from their being equiangular.

**Step 2.** Set A₁ = A and A₂ = B. Whenever a side AᵢAⱼ corresponding to a side CᵢCⱼ of one of the triangles has already been constructed, copy at Aᵢ and Aⱼ the angles at Cᵢ and Cⱼ of that triangle, placing both copied angles on the corresponding side of AᵢAⱼ [1.23]. The two original angles together are less than two right angles [1.17]; therefore the newly drawn straight lines meet on that side, at a point Aₖ [P5]. This constructs the triangle AᵢAⱼAₖ corresponding to CᵢCⱼCₖ.

**Step 3.** These two triangles have their two constructed angles equal. Since the angles of each triangle together equal two right angles, their remaining angles are also equal [1.32, CN2, CN3]. Consequently, their sides about corresponding equal angles are proportional [6.4]. Here 6.4 is the natural choice because equiangularity has already been established by the construction.

**Step 4.** Begin with the triangle on C₁C₂, whose corresponding side is AB, and continue the construction across the diagonals of the dissection. Whenever two original triangles adjoin along a diagonal, place their copies on opposite sides of the corresponding diagonal, retaining the original cyclic order of the vertices. Each attachment is possible by the construction in Step 2 [1.23, 1.17, P5]. In this way obtain the corresponding triangular division and its boundary A₁A₂…Aₙ, with A₁A₂ = AB.

**Step 5.** At each vertex, the angle of the whole rectilineal figure is the sum of the angles of the triangles incident there. Each such triangular angle equals its corresponding copied angle by Step 3. Adding these equal angles shows that the whole angles at Cᵢ and Aᵢ are equal, for every i [CN2].

**Step 6.** Fix a vertex Cᵢ. In their order through its interior angle, write the lengths of the incident sides and diagonals as e₀, e₁, …, eᵣ; thus e₀ and eᵣ are the two boundary sides at Cᵢ. Write e′₀, e′₁, …, e′ᵣ for the corresponding lengths at Aᵢ. Each successive pair belongs to a pair of corresponding equiangular triangles, so

eⱼ : eⱼ₊₁ = e′ⱼ : e′ⱼ₊₁

for every j from 0 to r − 1 [6.4]. Hence, ex aequali,

e₀ : eᵣ = e′₀ : e′ᵣ [5.22].

If only one triangle is incident at the vertex, this equality follows directly from 6.4. Thus, at every pair of corresponding equal angles, the two boundary sides are proportional.

**Step 7.** The figures C₁C₂…Cₙ and A₁A₂…Aₙ therefore have their angles severally equal and the sides about their equal angles proportional; hence they are similar [D6.1]. They are also similarly situated, because their corresponding vertices occur in the same cyclic order and their corresponding triangles were attached on matching sides of every diagonal. Since A₁A₂ is the given straight line AB, the required rectilineal figure has been described on AB.
statement: On a given straight line to describe a rectilineal figure similar and similarly situated to a given rectilineal figure.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let ABC and DEF be similar triangles, with A, B, C corresponding respectively to D, E, F. Choose BC and EF as an arbitrary pair of corresponding sides. Write [XYZ] for the area of triangle XYZ. By D6.1, ∠ABC = ∠DEF and AB:BC = DE:EF. By alternation (5.16),
AB:DE = BC:EF.

**Step 2.** By 6.11, construct a third proportional t to BC and EF, so that
BC:EF = EF:t.
This construction is the direct choice because duplicate ratio is defined by three proportional magnitudes (D5.9). Produce BC if necessary (P2), and mark G on the ray BC using the circle with centre B and radius t (P3). Thus BG = t and
BC:EF = EF:BG.
Join AG (P1).

**Step 3.** Combining the proportions in Steps 1 and 2 by 5.11 gives
AB:DE = EF:BG.
Thus the sides AB, BG and DE, EF are reciprocally proportional.

**Step 4.** Since the rays BG and BC coincide, ∠ABG = ∠ABC (CN4). Hence ∠ABG = ∠DEF by Step 1 and CN1. The triangles ABG and DEF therefore have an equal included angle and reciprocally proportional sides about that angle. By 6.15,
[ABG] = [DEF].

**Step 5.** Triangles ABC and ABG have the common vertex A and bases BC and BG on the same straight line, so they have the same height (D6.4). Consequently, by 6.1,
[ABC]:[ABG] = BC:BG.

**Step 6.** Since [ABG] = [DEF], the ratios [ABC]:[ABG] and [ABC]:[DEF] are equal (5.7). Combining this with Step 5 by 5.11 yields
[ABC]:[DEF] = BC:BG.

**Step 7.** Since BC:EF = EF:BG, the ratio BC:BG is the duplicate ratio of BC:EF (D5.9). Therefore [ABC]:[DEF] is the duplicate ratio of BC:EF. Since BC and EF were an arbitrary pair of corresponding sides, similar triangles are to one another in the duplicate ratio of their corresponding sides.
statement: Similar triangles are to one another in the duplicate ratio of the corresponding sides.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let A_1A_2…A_n and B_1B_2…B_n be similar polygons, their vertices being named in corresponding order. Their corresponding angles are equal, and the sides containing those angles are proportional (D6.1). If n = 3, each polygon already consists of one triangle, and the duplicate-ratio assertion is 6.19. Hence suppose n ≥ 4.

**Step 2.** Join A_1 to A_3,…,A_{n−1}, and B_1 to B_3,…,B_{n−1} (P1). These diagonals divide the polygons into corresponding fans
T_i = triangle A_1A_iA_{i+1}, and U_i = triangle B_1B_iB_{i+1},
for i = 2,…,n−1. Thus each division contains n−2 triangles. We shall prove that T_i and U_i are similar for every i.

**Step 3.** In T_2 and U_2, the included angles at A_2 and B_2 are equal, and
A_1A_2 : A_2A_3 = B_1B_2 : B_2B_3
(D6.1). Therefore these triangles are equiangular (6.6), and their corresponding sides are proportional (6.4); hence they are similar (D6.1). This use of 6.6 is direct: an equal included angle and proportional containing sides are precisely the data already given.

**Step 4.** Suppose T_{i−1} and U_{i−1} have been proved similar, where 3 ≤ i ≤ n−1. Their angles at A_i and B_i are equal (D6.1). Subtract these equal angles from the equal polygon angles at those vertices. The remaining angles are therefore equal:
∠A_1A_iA_{i+1} = ∠B_1B_iB_{i+1}
(CN3).

**Step 5.** The preceding pair of similar triangles gives
A_1A_i : A_{i−1}A_i = B_1B_i : B_{i−1}B_i
(6.4). The similarity of the original polygons gives
A_{i−1}A_i : A_iA_{i+1} = B_{i−1}B_i : B_iB_{i+1}
(D6.1). Consequently, ex aequali,
A_1A_i : A_iA_{i+1} = B_1B_i : B_iB_{i+1}
(5.22). Together with the angle equality in Step 4, this makes T_i and U_i equiangular (6.6), with corresponding sides proportional (6.4), and therefore similar (D6.1). Starting with Step 3 and repeating this argument proves the similarity of every corresponding pair. The polygons have thus been divided into similar triangles equal in multitude.

**Step 6.** Write t_i and u_i for the areas of T_i and U_i. For each i = 2,…,n−2, the adjacent triangles T_i and T_{i+1} share the side A_1A_{i+1}, while U_i and U_{i+1} share its corresponding side B_1B_{i+1}. By 6.19, both ratios t_i : u_i and t_{i+1} : u_{i+1} are the duplicate ratio of the very same ratio
A_1A_{i+1} : B_1B_{i+1}
(D5.9). They are therefore equal; chaining these equalities gives
 t_2 : u_2 = t_3 : u_3 = … = t_{n−1} : u_{n−1}
(5.11). Using the shared diagonals allows 6.19 to apply directly, without an auxiliary proportional-line construction.

**Step 7.** When any number of antecedents have the same ratio to their respective consequents, the sum of the antecedents has that ratio to the sum of the consequents (5.12). Hence
(t_2 + … + t_{n−1}) : (u_2 + … + u_{n−1}) = t_i : u_i
for every i. The two sums are exactly the areas of the respective polygons, by the divisions in Step 2. Thus every corresponding pair of triangles is in the same ratio as the whole polygons.

**Step 8.** In particular, the ratio of the polygons equals t_2 : u_2. Since T_2 and U_2 are similar and have corresponding sides A_1A_2 and B_1B_2, this triangle ratio is the duplicate ratio of A_1A_2 : B_1B_2 (6.19). Therefore the polygon has to the polygon the duplicate ratio of that corresponding side to its corresponding side (5.11). The initial side A_1A_2 could have been any side, with B_1B_2 its correspondent. Thus the conclusion holds for any corresponding sides. The similar polygons are divided into similar triangles equal in multitude and in the same ratio as the wholes, and the wholes are in the duplicate ratio of corresponding sides, as required.
statement: Similar polygons are divided into similar triangles, and into triangles equal in multitude and in the same ratio as the wholes, and the polygon has to the polygon a ratio duplicate of that which the corresponding side has to the corresponding  side.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let F and G each be similar to the rectilineal figure H. Match the vertices and sides of F and G through their respective correspondences with H. By the definition of similarity, each given correspondence has equal corresponding angles and proportional sides about those angles. [D6.1]

**Step 2.** Take any three corresponding angles, one in each figure. The angle in F equals the angle in H, and the angle in G equals that same angle in H. Therefore the angles in F and G are equal. Since the corresponding angles were arbitrary, F and G have their angles severally equal. [D6.1, CN1]

**Step 3.** Let a, b be the sides about any chosen angle in F; let c, d be their corresponding sides in H; and let e, f be their corresponding sides in G, taken in the same order. The given similarities yield a:b = c:d and e:f = c:d. Ratios which are the same with the same ratio are also the same with one another; hence a:b = e:f. Thus the sides of F and G about every pair of corresponding equal angles are proportional. The direct path is 5.11, since the two ratios already agree with the same ratio in H. [D6.1, 5.11]

**Step 4.** Consequently F and G have their angles severally equal and the sides about the equal angles proportional. They are therefore similar. Hence figures which are similar to the same rectilineal figure are also similar to one another. [D6.1]
statement: Figures which are similar to the same rectilineal figure are also similar to one another.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let the four straight lines be a, b, c, d, and let the rectilineal figures described upon them be F, G, H, K, respectively. Suppose F and G are similar and similarly described upon a and b, and H and K upon c and d; thus these lines are corresponding sides. We must prove that a:b = c:d if and only if F:G = H:K. [D6.1, D5.6]

**Step 2.** Construct third proportionals x and y such that a:b = b:x and c:d = d:y. [6.11] Consequently, a:x and c:y are the duplicate ratios of a:b and c:d, respectively. [D5.9] Therefore F:G = a:x and H:K = c:y. [6.20] This is our path choice: express duplicate ratios by ordinary ratios of constructed lines, using the theorem for general rectilineal figures.

**Step 3.** First suppose a:b = c:d. Since a:b = b:x and c:d = d:y, we also have b:x = d:y. [5.11] Applying ex aequali to the triples a, b, x and c, d, y gives a:x = c:y. [5.22] Together with Step 2, this gives F:G = H:K. [5.11] Thus proportional straight lines yield proportional figures.

**Step 4.** Conversely, suppose F:G = H:K. Step 2 then gives a:x = c:y. [5.11] Construct a fourth proportional e to a, b, c, so that a:b = c:e; then construct a third proportional f to c, e, so that c:e = e:f. [6.12, 6.11]

**Step 5.** Since b:x = a:b = c:e = e:f, we have b:x = e:f. [5.11] Hence, from a:b = c:e and b:x = e:f, ex aequali gives a:x = c:f. [5.22]

**Step 6.** Comparing Steps 4 and 5 gives c:f = c:y. [5.11] Magnitudes to which the same magnitude has the same ratio are equal; therefore f = y. [5.9] Substituting this equality into c:e = e:f gives c:e = e:y. [5.7, 5.11] We consequently have both c:d = d:y and c:e = e:y.

**Step 7.** Inverting c:d = d:y gives d:c = y:d; inversion preserves equality of ratios by the defining equimultiple comparisons. [D5.5] Thus d:c = y:d and c:e = e:y. These are precisely the perturbed proportions between the triples d, c, e and e, y, d. Perturbed ex aequali therefore gives d:e = e:d. [5.23] This form of ex aequali is chosen because the matching ratios occur in perturbed order.

**Step 8.** In the equality d:e = e:d, take one-fold multiples of all four terms. The definition of equal ratios requires the comparison of d with e to agree with the comparison of e with d. Neither strict inequality can satisfy this, so d = e. [D5.5] Consequently c:e = c:d, and a:b = c:e yields a:b = c:d. [5.7, 5.11] Thus proportional figures yield proportional straight lines. Both directions are proved. [D5.6]
statement: If four straight lines be proportional, the rectilineal figures similar and similarly described upon them will also be proportional; and, if the rectilineal figures similar and similarly described upon them be proportional, the straight lines will themselves also be proportional.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let the given equiangular parallelograms be ABCD and AEFG, placed with their equal angles DAB and GAE coinciding, so that AB and AE lie along one ray and AD and AG along another. Such placement preserves their areas and side lengths (CN4). Write P and Q for their respective areas. We shall insert an intermediate parallelogram: this makes the equal-height theorem 6.1 directly applicable to both comparisons.

**Step 2.** Through E draw a straight line parallel to AD, and through D draw a straight line parallel to AB; let these meet at H (1.31). Then AEHD is a parallelogram. Denote its area by R.

**Step 3.** The parallelograms ABCD and AEHD have bases AB and AE on the same straight line, and their opposite sides CD and DH lie on the same parallel through D. They therefore have the same height. Hence
P : R = AB : AE
by 6.1.

**Step 4.** Regard AD and AG as the bases of AEHD and AEFG. These bases lie on the same straight line, while their opposite sides EH and EF lie on the same parallel through E. Thus these parallelograms also have the same height, and
R : Q = AD : AG
by 6.1.

**Step 5.** Find a fourth proportional straight line t to AD, AG, and AE, so that
AD : AG = AE : t
(6.12). Combining this with Step 4 gives
R : Q = AE : t
(5.11). Thus the three areas P, R, Q and the three straight lines AB, AE, t have their successive ratios equal.

**Step 6.** By proportion ex aequali,
P : Q = AB : t
(5.22). The ratio AB : t is compounded of AB : AE and AE : t: the sizes of these successive ratios, multiplied together, give the size of the first-to-last ratio (D6.5). Since AE : t = AD : AG, it follows that P : Q is compounded of AB : AE and AD : AG. These are the ratios of the corresponding sides about the equal angles. Therefore equiangular parallelograms have to one another the ratio compounded of the ratios of their sides.
statement: Equiangular parallelograms have to one another the ratio compounded of the ratios of their sides.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let ABCD be a parallelogram with diameter AC, and let O lie between A and C. Through O draw EG parallel to AD, meeting AB at E and CD at G; also draw HF parallel to AB, meeting AD at H and BC at F [1.31]. Then EG is also parallel to BC, and HF to CD [1.30]. Thus AEOH and OFCG are the two parallelograms about the diameter.

**Step 2.** The angle at A of AEOH coincides with the angle at A of ABCD, and the angle at C of OFCG coincides with the angle at C of ABCD [CN4]. The angles AEO and OFC each equal ABC, by the parallel lines [1.29]. Since opposite angles of a parallelogram are equal, the remaining corresponding angles are equal as well [1.34, CN1]. Consequently both smaller parallelograms are equiangular with ABCD, with respective vertex correspondences
A,E,O,H ↔ A,B,C,D,
and O,F,C,G ↔ A,B,C,D.

**Step 3.** Triangles AEO and ABC are equiangular: their angles at A coincide, while their other corresponding angles are equal by EO ∥ BC [CN4, 1.29]. Path choice: apply 6.4 directly, since equiangularity is already established. Taking the sides about the equal angles E and B in both orders gives
AE:EO = AB:BC,
and EO:AE = BC:AB [6.4].

**Step 4.** Opposite sides of the two parallelograms are equal:
AE = OH, EO = HA, AB = CD, and BC = DA [1.34]. Substituting these equal sides into the proportions of Step 3 gives
AE:EO = AB:BC,
EO:OH = BC:CD,
OH:HA = CD:DA,
HA:AE = DA:AB.
Thus the sides about every pair of corresponding equal angles are proportional. Together with Step 2, this proves that AEOH is similar to ABCD [D6.1].

**Step 5.** Triangles OFC and ABC are likewise equiangular: their angles at C coincide, and their other corresponding angles are equal because OF ∥ AB [CN4, 1.29]. Applying 6.4 to the sides about the equal angles F and B, in both orders, gives
OF:FC = AB:BC,
and FC:OF = BC:AB [6.4].

**Step 6.** Opposite sides give OF = CG and FC = GO, while AB = CD and BC = DA [1.34]. Hence the proportions of Step 5 yield
OF:FC = AB:BC,
FC:CG = BC:CD,
CG:GO = CD:DA,
GO:OF = DA:AB.
Combined with the corresponding angle equalities of Step 2, these proportions prove that OFCG is similar to ABCD [D6.1].

**Step 7.** Both AEOH and OFCG are similar to the same rectilineal figure ABCD; therefore they are similar to one another [6.21]. Thus the parallelograms about the diameter are similar both to the whole and to one another.
statement: In any parallelogram the parallelograms about the diameter are similar both to the whole and to one another.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let F be the given rectilineal figure to which the required figure must be similar, and G the given rectilineal figure to which it must be equal. Choose a side a of F. Construct squares Q and R equal in area to F and G respectively, and denote their sides by p and q. [2.14]

**Step 2.** To the three straight lines p, q, a construct a fourth proportional b, so that
p : q = a : b. [6.12]

**Step 3.** On b construct a rectilineal figure H similar and similarly situated to F, with b corresponding to the side a of F. [6.18]

**Step 4.** The squares Q and R are similar: their corresponding angles are equal because all are right angles, and their sides about equal angles are proportional because each square has all its sides equal. [D1.22, P4, D5.5, D6.1] Regard them as similarly described on p and q. Thus Q and R are similar figures described on p and q, while F and H are similar and similarly described on a and b. Since p : q = a : b, it follows that
Q : R = F : H. [6.22]
The direct ratio-transfer proposition 6.22 is the natural choice here because the construction has supplied precisely its four proportional straight lines and two pairs of similar figures.

**Step 5.** Substituting Q = F and R = G into this proportion gives
F : G = F : H. [D5.5]
Magnitudes to which the same magnitude has the same ratio are equal; therefore G = H. [5.9] By Step 3, H is also similar to F. Hence the one figure H is similar to the given rectilineal figure F and equal to the other given rectilineal figure G, as required. [6.18, 5.9]
statement: To construct one and the same figure similar to a given rectilineal figure and equal to another given rectilineal figure.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let ABCD be the whole parallelogram and AEFG the parallelogram taken away, with vertices named in corresponding order and common angle at A. Thus E lies on AB and G lies on AD. Since the parallelograms are similar and similarly situated, AE:EF = AB:BC and ∠AEF = ∠ABC. [Hypotheses; D6.1]

**Step 2.** Join AF and AC. [P1] We use the side–angle–side criterion 6.6 directly: the proportional sides and equal included angles in Step 1 already supply its hypotheses for triangles AEF and ABC, so no auxiliary parallelogram is needed.

**Step 3.** Triangles AEF and ABC are therefore equiangular, with A corresponding to A, E to B, and F to C. Hence ∠EAF = ∠BAC. Since AE and AB are the same ray, this gives ∠BAF = ∠BAC. [6.6; Step 1]

**Step 4.** The rays AF and AC both lie inside the common angle DAB. If they were distinct, one of ∠BAF and ∠BAC would be a proper part of the other and therefore smaller, contradicting Step 3. [CN5] Thus A, F, and C are collinear. Since AEFG is contained in ABCD, its diameter AF lies on the diameter AC of the whole. Therefore the parallelogram taken away is about the same diameter with the whole, as required.
statement: If from a parallelogram there be taken away a parallelogram similar and similarly situated to the whole and having a common angle with it, it is about the same diameter with the whole.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let AB be bisected at M, and let MBCD be the prescribed parallelogram on MB, with vertices named consecutively. Through A draw AE parallel to MD, meeting CD produced beyond D at E. Thus AMDE is the parallelogram applied to AM, and its defect on AB is MBCD. [1.10, 1.31, P2]

**Step 2.** The parallelograms AMDE and MBCD have equal corresponding sides: AM = MB, MD = BC, DE = AM = MB = CD, and EA = MD. Their corresponding angles are also equal, since their sides are correspondingly parallel. Hence AMDE is similar to its defect MBCD and is an admissible application. In particular, ED = DC. Denote its area by U. [1.29, 1.30, 1.34, CN1, D6.1]

**Step 3.** Take any admissible application AXGH, where X is an interior point of AB, and write its defect as XBFG, with vertices named consecutively. By the stipulated similar situation, BF lies on the ray BC, AH lies on the ray AE, and H, G, F are collinear on a line parallel to AB. Similarity gives XB : BF = MB : BC. Consequently, if X lies between M and B, then BF < BC and XBFG is contained in MBCD; if X lies between A and M, then BF > BC and MBCD is contained in XBFG. If X = M, then BF = BC, so the application coincides with AMDE. Denote the area of AXGH by V. [D6.1, 1.30, CN5, 5.14, CN4]

**Step 4.** First suppose X lies between M and B. Let K be the intersection of HG with MD, and let XG produced meet DC at L. Then K lies between M and D, and L between D and C. Since XBFG is similar and similarly situated to MBCD and shares its angle at B, G lies on the diameter BD. Therefore the complements MXGK and GFCL are equal in area. Our path choice is to use the common-diameter criterion followed by equality of complements: the nested similar defects already satisfy these hypotheses, giving a direct dissection comparison. [P2, 6.26, 1.43]

**Step 5.** The parallelograms HKDE and KFCD have equal bases ED and DC and lie between the same parallels EDC and HGF. Therefore they are equal in area. We use equality of parallelograms on equal bases here because those bases and parallels are already present. Writing [W] for the area of a figure W, the dissections give
U = [AMKH] + [HKDE]
  = [AMKH] + [KFCD]
  = [AMKH] + [GFCL] + [KGLD]
  = [AMKH] + [MXGK] + [KGLD]
  = V + [KGLD].
Since KGLD is a nondegenerate parallelogram, U > V. [1.36, CN2, CN5]

**Step 6.** Now suppose X lies between A and M. Let MD produced meet HG at K, and let XG meet ED at L. Here K lies beyond D, and L lies between E and D. The smaller parallelogram MBCD is similar and similarly situated to XBFG and shares its angle at B; hence D lies on the diameter BG. The complements XMDL and DCFK in XBFG are therefore equal in area. [P2, 6.26, 1.43]

**Step 7.** The parallelograms EDKH and DCFK have equal bases ED and DC and lie between the same parallels EDC and HGF, so they are equal in area. Consequently,
U = [AXLE] + [XMDL]
  = [AXLE] + [DCFK]
  = [AXLE] + [EDKH]
  = [AXLE] + [ELGH] + [LDKG]
  = V + [LDKG].
The parallelogram LDKG is nondegenerate, so again U > V. [1.36, CN2, CN5]

**Step 8.** Thus every admissible application whose base ends away from M is strictly smaller than AMDE, while the application whose base ends at M coincides with it. Since AMDE is applied to half of AB and is similar to its defect, it is the greatest of all the stated parallelograms. [CN4, CN5]
statement: Of all the parallelograms applied to the same straight line and deficient by parallelogrammic figures similar and similarly situated to that described on the half of the straight line, that parallelogram is greatest which is applied to the half of the straight line and is similar to the defect.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let AB be the given straight line, F the given rectilineal figure, and S the given parallelogram specifying the defect. Bisect AB at E (1.10), and on EB construct a parallelogram EBCD similar and similarly situated to S (6.18). Call this parallelogram H, and write [Z] for the area of a figure Z. By hypothesis, [F] ≤ [H].

**Step 2.** Produce CD through D, and draw through A a parallel to ED, meeting the produced line at G (P2, 1.31). The parallelograms AEDG and EBCD have equal bases AE and EB and lie between the same parallels AB and GC; therefore their areas are equal (1.36). If [F] = [H], AEDG is the required application, with EBCD as its defect. Moreover, 6.27 establishes the necessity of the stated upper bound: the half-line application is greatest among applications with the specified similar defect. It remains to treat [F] < [H].

**Step 3.** Construction choice: use 6.25, since it directly supplies both prescribed area and prescribed similarity. First construct a parallelogram J similar to H and equal to F (6.25). This will allow the excess of H over F to be represented by an actual rectilineal remainder.

**Step 4.** The adjacent sides of J corresponding to DC and DE are both shorter than those sides of H. Indeed, similarity makes the corresponding adjacent sides proportional (D6.1), and consequently both pairs compare in the same sense (5.14). If they were equal, a copy placed at the corresponding angle D would coincide with H; if greater, it would contain H. Either possibility contradicts [J] = [F] < [H] (CN4, CN5). Cut off the two shorter lengths along DC and DE and complete a copy of J inside H by parallels (1.3, 1.31). This copy has the same area as J: the triangles formed by its adjacent sides agree with the corresponding triangles of J by 1.4, and those triangles are halves of their parallelograms by 1.34 (CN2). Henceforth let J denote this copy at D.

**Step 5.** Let R be the remainder of H outside J. Since J occupies the corner D, R is a rectilineal figure (D1.19), and [R] + [F] = [H] (CN2). Also, 0 < [R] < [H] (CN5). Construct a parallelogram K similar to H and equal to R (6.25). By the same side comparison and copying construction as in Step 4, place K inside H at D, similarly situated to H. Denote it DUXV, with U on DC, V on DE, and X opposite D. Thus
[H] − [DUXV] = [F] (CN3).

**Step 6.** Join DB (P1). Since DUXV is similar and similarly situated to H and has the common angle D, it is about the same diameter DB; in particular, X lies on DB (6.26).

**Step 7.** Produce UX to meet EB at T. Produce VX in one direction to meet BC at W, and in the other direction to meet AG at L (P2). The parallelisms of the construction, together with transitivity of parallelism (1.30), make ATXL and TBWX parallelograms. Their union is the parallelogram ABWL on the whole given line AB. Thus ATXL is applied to AB with defect TBWX; it remains to establish its area and the similarity of its defect.

**Step 8.** Within H, TBWX is the parallelogram about the diameter DB opposite DUXV. Therefore TBWX is similar to H (6.24), and hence similar to the given parallelogram S (6.21).

**Step 9.** The other two parallelograms in the division of H, namely ETXV and UCWX, are the complements about the diameter DB. Consequently,
[ETXV] = [UCWX] (1.43).

**Step 10.** The parallelograms AEVL and EBWV have equal bases AE and EB and lie between the same parallels AB and LW. The equal-base theorem applies directly, giving
[AEVL] = [EBWV] (1.36).

**Step 11.** Add the equalities from Steps 9 and 10 (CN2). Using the indicated divisions of ATXL and H, and then Step 5, gives
[ATXL] = [AEVL] + [ETXV]
= [EBWV] + [UCWX]
= [H] − [DUXV]
= [F] (CN3).
Therefore ATXL is equal to the given rectilineal figure and is applied to AB deficient by TBWX, which is similar to S by Step 8. Together with the equality case in Step 2, this completes the construction under precisely the stated bound.
statement: To a given straight line to apply a parallelogram equal to a given rectilineal figure and deficient by a parallelogrammic figure similar to a given one: thus the given rectilineal figure must not be greater than the parallelogram described on the half of the straight line and similar to the defect.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let AB be the given straight line, let ℱ be the given rectilineal figure, and let 𝒟 be the given parallelogram. Write [X] for the area of a figure X. Bisect AB at M (1.10), and on MB construct a parallelogram MBRS similar to 𝒟 (6.18). Denote this parallelogram, also named SRBM, by Q. We shall construct a larger similar parallelogram and use its equal complements; this makes the required excess appear directly.

**Step 2.** Construct a parallelogram equal to ℱ (1.45), and adjoin it externally to Q along a nonzero boundary segment, with their interiors disjoint. Their union is a rectilineal figure 𝒢 satisfying [𝒢] = [Q] + [ℱ] (CN2).

**Step 3.** By 6.25 construct a parallelogram similar to Q and equal to 𝒢. Set a copy of it in the angle RSM, calling it STUV, with its corresponding sides ST and SV on the rays SR and SM respectively. This setting is constructed by copying the adjacent side-lengths onto the rays and completing parallels (P2, 1.3, 1.31). Corresponding angles agree by 1.29; joining the diagonals between the endpoints of those adjacent sides gives equal triangles by 1.4, and hence equal parallelograms by 1.34 and CN2 (P1). Thus STUV is similar and similarly situated to Q, and [STUV] = [Q] + [ℱ] (6.25, CN1).

**Step 4.** Similarity gives ST:SV = SR:SM (D6.1). Consequently ST compares with SR in the same way that SV compares with SM (5.14). If ST were no greater than SR, then SV would be no greater than SM, and STUV would be contained in Q or coincide with it. It could not then have greater area than Q (CN5). But [STUV] = [Q] + [ℱ] > [Q] (CN5). Therefore ST > SR and SV > SM: R lies between S and T, M lies between S and V, and Q lies within STUV.

**Step 5.** Join SU (P1). Since Q is similar and similarly situated to STUV and has the common angle at S, it is about the same diagonal SU; hence B lies on SU (6.26). Produce MB beyond B to meet TU at X, and RB beyond B to meet VU at Y (P2). The parallel sides of the two parallelograms give the resulting parallel grid (1.30). In particular, M, B, X occur in that order, and the four parts of STUV are Q, RTXB, MBYV, and BXUY.

**Step 6.** Through A draw a parallel to TU, meeting VU produced beyond V at Z (1.31, P2). Then AXUZ is a parallelogram, partitioned into the three parallelograms AMVZ, MBYV, and BXUY; their opposite sides are parallel by construction and 1.30. Its base AX contains AB and extends beyond B to X.

**Step 7.** In STUV, the parallelograms Q and BXUY are about the diagonal SU. The other two parts, RTXB and MBYV, are therefore its complements, so [RTXB] = [MBYV] (1.43).

**Step 8.** Since AM = MB, the parallelograms AMVZ and MBYV have equal bases and lie between the same parallels AB and ZU. Hence [AMVZ] = [MBYV] (1.36), and therefore [AMVZ] = [RTXB] (CN1). Here 1.36 is the natural first choice: equal bases between the same parallels already give the required equality, without a proportional-area argument.

**Step 9.** Subtract Q from the equality [STUV] = [Q] + [ℱ]. The partition in Step 5 gives
[ℱ] = [RTXB] + [MBYV] + [BXUY] (CN3).
Replace RTXB by the equal parallelogram AMVZ from Step 8. By addition of equals and the partition in Step 6,
[ℱ] = [AMVZ] + [MBYV] + [BXUY] = [AXUZ] (CN2, CN1).

**Step 10.** The parallelograms BXUY and Q are about the diagonal of STUV, and are therefore similar to one another (6.24). Since Q is similar to 𝒟, BXUY is similar to 𝒟 (6.21). The line BY separates AXUZ into the parallelogram ABYZ on the given line AB and the excess BXUY beyond B. Thus AXUZ is a parallelogram equal to ℱ, applied to AB and exceeding by a parallelogram similar to the given one, as required.
statement: To a given straight line to apply a parallelogram equal to a given rectilineal figure and exceeding by a parallelogrammic figure similar to a given one.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let AB be the given finite straight line. By 2.11, cut AB at an interior point C so that the rectangle contained by AB and CB equals the square on AC. This rectangle–square construction is the direct route because it supplies exactly the equality needed for a three-term proportion. [2.11]

**Step 2.** By the converse of 6.17, applied with AB and CB as the extremes and AC as the mean,
AB : AC = AC : CB.
The three-line criterion applies directly because the given rectangle equals a square on the mean. [6.17]

**Step 3.** Since AC is a proper part of AB, AB > AC. In the proportion just obtained, the first magnitude therefore exceeds the third; hence the second exceeds the fourth. Thus AC > CB. [CN5, 5.14]

**Step 4.** Consequently, as the whole AB is to the greater segment AC, so is AC to the less segment CB. Therefore AB has been cut at C in extreme and mean ratio, as required. [D6.3]
statement: To cut a given finite straight line in extreme and mean ratio.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let ABC be right-angled at A. Denote by F_BC, F_AB, and F_AC the areas of the similar and similarly described rectilineal figures on BC, AB, and AC, respectively; these supporting sides are corresponding sides (D6.1). Path choice: transfer the established equality for squares to the given figures by the general polygon-ratio theorem.

**Step 2.** Describe squares on BC, AB, and AC, and denote their areas by Q_BC, Q_AB, and Q_AC (1.46). These squares are similar: their angles are equal right angles, and their corresponding sides are proportional because all the sides within each square are equal (D1.22, P4, D6.1).

**Step 3.** By 6.20, each of the ratios F_AB : F_BC and Q_AB : Q_BC is the duplicate ratio of AB : BC. Likewise, each of F_AC : F_BC and Q_AC : Q_BC is the duplicate ratio of AC : BC. Therefore, by 5.11,
F_AB : F_BC = Q_AB : Q_BC,
and
F_AC : F_BC = Q_AC : Q_BC.
Here 6.20 is the natural choice because the given figures are arbitrary polygons, not necessarily triangles.

**Step 4.** Adding the antecedents in these two proportions, while retaining their respective common consequents, gives
(F_AB + F_AC) : F_BC = (Q_AB + Q_AC) : Q_BC
(5.24).

**Step 5.** Since ABC is right-angled at A, the square on BC equals the squares on AB and AC together:
Q_AB + Q_AC = Q_BC
(1.47). Substitution into Step 4 therefore gives
(F_AB + F_AC) : F_BC = Q_BC : Q_BC.

**Step 6.** Apply the definition of equal ratios, taking both multipliers to be one. Since the two magnitudes in Q_BC : Q_BC are equal, the corresponding magnitudes F_AB + F_AC and F_BC must also be equal (D5.5). Thus F_BC = F_AB + F_AC: the figure on the side subtending the right angle equals the similar and similarly described figures on the sides containing that angle, taken together.
statement: In right - angled triangles the figure on the side subtending the right angle is equal to the similar and similarly described figures on the sides containing the right angle.

proof:
**Step 1.** Label the triangles ABC and DCE in their prescribed adjoining placement at C, with AB:AC = DC:DE, AB parallel to DC, and AC parallel to DE. In this placement CA lies inside angle BCD, and CB and CE lie on opposite sides of CD. We must prove that BC and CE form one straight line. [Given proportionality and placement.]

**Step 2.** Since AB is parallel to DC, the transversal AC gives ∠BAC = ∠ACD. Since AC is parallel to DE, the transversal CD gives ∠ACD = ∠CDE. Hence ∠BAC = ∠CDE. [1.29, CN1]

**Step 3.** The triangles ABC and DCE therefore have equal included angles and proportional sides about those angles. They are consequently equiangular, and in particular ∠ABC = ∠DCE, these angles being opposite the corresponding sides AC and DE. The direct choice is 6.6, because precisely its included-angle and two-side hypotheses have now been established. [6.6]

**Step 4.** Since AB is parallel to DC, the transversal BC makes the interior angles ABC and BCD on the same side together equal to two right angles. Thus ∠ABC + ∠BCD equals two right angles. [1.29]

**Step 5.** Add ∠BCD to the equal angles ∠ABC and ∠DCE from Step 3. Using Step 4, it follows that ∠DCE + ∠BCD equals two right angles. [CN2, CN1]

**Step 6.** At C, the straight lines CB and CE lie on opposite sides of CD and make with it the adjacent angles BCD and DCE, whose sum is two right angles. Therefore CB and CE are in a straight line. Thus the remaining sides BC and CE of the two triangles form one straight line, as required. [1.14]
statement: If two triangles having two sides proportional to two sides be placed together at one angle so that their corresponding sides are also parallel, the remaining sides of the triangles will be in a straight line.

proof:
**Step 1.** Let θ and φ be angles in two equal circles, either both at their centres or both at their circumferences, and let a and b be the respective arcs on which they stand (D3.9). We use 3.26 directly: it converts equal angles into equal intercepted arcs in both cases, so it naturally applies to subdivisions obtained by angle-bisection. We shall establish the required proportion by the equimultiple criterion D5.5.

**Step 2.** First, comparisons between such angles agree with comparisons between their intercepted arcs. Equal angles intercept equal arcs by 3.26. If one angle is greater than another, construct an angle equal to the smaller inside the greater, sharing one boundary side (1.23), and extend its other side to the circumference (P2). Its intercepted arc is a proper part of the arc intercepted by the greater angle, and equals the arc intercepted by the smaller angle (3.26). The greater angle therefore intercepts the greater arc (CN5). Interchanging the angles gives the corresponding assertion for a smaller angle. Thus greater, equal, and smaller angles intercept respectively greater, equal, and smaller arcs.

**Step 3.** Let m and n be arbitrary positive whole-number multipliers. Choose a power of two k not smaller than either m or n. By repeated bisection, divide each of θ and φ into k equal adjacent angles, extending the dividing rays to the circumference (1.9, P2). Write θ₀ and φ₀ for one small angle in the respective divisions. The corresponding k successive arcs in each circle are equal, since their angles are equal (3.26); write a₀ and b₀ for one arc in the respective divisions. Hence, by the definition of a multiple,
θ = kθ₀, φ = kφ₀, a = ka₀, and b = kb₀ (D5.2).

**Step 4.** Take the first m adjacent small angles within θ and the first n within φ. Denote the resulting angles by Θ and Φ, and their intercepted arcs by A and B. Then
Θ = mθ₀, Φ = nφ₀, A = ma₀, and B = nb₀ (D3.9, D5.2).
Because m and n are at most k, these auxiliary angles and arcs remain within the original angles and arcs. They therefore are genuine angles of the chosen kind, standing on the indicated arcs. By Step 2, the comparison between Θ and Φ agrees with the comparison between A and B (1.23, 3.26, CN5).

**Step 5.** Taking k-fold sums and applying the addition rule for equimultiples gives
kΘ = mθ, kΦ = nφ, kA = ma, and kB = nb (5.1).
Equality is preserved under this common repetition by addition of equals (CN2). Strict inequality is also preserved: the larger magnitude consists of the smaller together with a positive remainder, and repeating both leaves a positive repeated remainder (5.1, CN5). Consequently, according as Θ exceeds, equals, or falls short of Φ, both mθ compared with nφ and ma compared with nb have that same relation. Thus mθ and nφ alike exceed, are alike equal to, or alike fall short of ma and nb respectively taken in corresponding order. These unrestricted multiples are sums; they need not fit within a single angle or circumference.

**Step 6.** Since m and n were arbitrary, D5.5 gives θ : φ = a : b. The construction and comparison apply both when the two angles stand at the centres and when they stand at the circumferences. Therefore, in equal circles, angles have the same ratio as the circumferences on which they stand, in either case.
statement: In equal circles angles have the same ratio as the circumferences on which they stand, whether they stand at the centres or at the circumferences.
